Molecular evidence and diversity of the spotted-fever group Rickettsia spp. in
small mammals from natural, suburban and urban areas of Eastern Slovakia
Ivana Heglasováa,b,⁎ , Bronislava Víchováa , Jasna Kraljika,c , Ladislav Mošanskýa , Dana Miklisováa ,
Michal Stankoa,c
a Institute of Parasitology, Slovak Academy of Sciences, Hlinkova 3, 040 01 Košice, Slovakia
b Department of Zoology, Faculty of Natural Sciences, Comenius University, Mlynská dolina B-1, 842 15 Bratislava, Slovakia
c Institute of Zoology, Slovak Academy of Sciences, Dúbravská cesta 9, 845 06 Bratislava, Slovakia
A R T I C L E I N F O

A B S T R A C T
Rickettsiae of the spotted fever group are considered as emerging pathogens; ticks, fleas and mites are known to
be their vectors. However, the prevalence and species diversity of rickettsiae in small mammals and the role of
these hosts in the circulation of bacteria are much less studied. During 2014–2016, a total of 250 small mammals
(Apodemus agrarius, Apodemus flavicollis, Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, Crocidura leucodon, Crocidura
suaveolens, Micromys minutus, Microtus arvalis, Microtus subterraneus, Neomys fodiens and Sorex minutus) were
captured in natural, suburban and urban habitats of eastern Slovakia. Ear biopsies of 245 individuals were
examined for the presence of SFG rickettsiae by molecular methods. The overall prevalence of Rickettsia spp. in
small mammals was
. The predominant species, Rickettsia helvetica was confirmed in the striped field mouse
(A. agrarius), the yellow-necked mouse (A. flavicollis), the bank vole (M. glareolus) and the common vole (M.
arvalis) in natural and suburban habitats, followed by Rickettsia sp. closely related to R. felis identified in A.
flavicollis captured in a suburban habitat. Finally, R. slovaca was found in only one yellow-necked mouse (A.
flavicollis) captured in a natural habitat, with the sympatric occurrence of Dermacentor marginatus and
Dermacentor reticulatus ticks. We assume the presence of R. slovaca especially in sites with the occurrence of
Dermacentor spp. All small mammals captured in the urban habitat tested were negative for the presence of
rickettsiae. This study brings the first molecular evidence of R. slovaca in a rodent captured in Slovakia. Rickettsia
sp. closely related to R. felis was first time detected in A. flavicollis in suburban site of Slovakia.
The highest species diversity of rickettsiae was observed in A. flavicollis, and the highest prevalence of bac-
teria was recorded in M. glareolus. The highest occurrence of rickettsiae-positive small mammals was recorded
during the spring and autumn months, May, June and September, respectively. This may be related with the
seasonal activity of the tick vectors. This study confirms the long-term persistence of Rickettsia spp. in small
mammals in natural and suburban habitats of Slovakia.
Some rodent species that have a wider ecological valency may contribute to the maintenance, circulation and
dissemination of rickettsiae within and out the natural foci more significantly than those species that have
narrower relation to the certain type of habitat.
1. Introduction
The genus Rickettsia (Rickettsiaceae, Rickettsiales) includes Gram-
negative obligate, intracellular, aerobic
\alpha
-Proteobacteria invading
hosts’ eukaryotic cells. Species of the genus Rickettsia are divided into
two groups: the spotted fever group (SFG) and the typhus group (TG)
(Raoult et al., 2005). The main vectors of rickettsiae are blood-sucking
arthropods, mainly ticks, but also fleas, mites and human body lice. The
highest occurrence of rickettsiae in ticks was detected in early spring
and autumn (Řeháček et al., 1972). Řeháček et al. (1972) suggested that
rickettsiae are able to hibernate in ticks. The most important vectors
and probably also the main reservoirs of rickettsiae in Southern, Wes-
tern and Central Europe are Dermacentor marginatus and Dermacentor
reticulatus ticks (Řeháček et al., 1972, 1977; Raoult et al., 2002).
Small rodents, hosting a wide spectrum of ectoparasites and ar-
thropod vectors, are the most significant reservoirs of rickettsiae, many

of which are responsible for serious zoonotic diseases (rickettsioses) of
humans and animals (Řeháček et al., 1992; Burri et al., 2014; Han et al.,
2015; Imhoff et al., 2015). Rickettsioses belong among the most fre-
quent vector-borne infections in Europe (Fournier et al., 2012).
In Slovakia, six rickettsial species/strains of the SFG have thus far
been identified by serological examination and/or different molecular
methods. Among the identified species are Rickettsia helvetica, Rickettsia
slovaca, Rickettsia raoultii, Rickettsia monacensis strain IRS3 and IRS4,
Rickettsia conorii and Rickettsia africae (Brezina et al., 1969; Řehácek
et al., 1975; Boldiš et al., 2008; Špitalská et al., 2012, 2014; Sekeyová
et al., 2013). Recently, Rickettsia sp., closely related to Rickettsia felis,
was detected in Slovakia (Špitalská et al., 2015). These species of
rickettsiae are usually transmitted by the ticks, but R. africae and R. felis
have also been identified in fleas (Sekeyová et al., 2013; Špitalská et al.,
R. slovaca was isolated for the first time in 1968 from D. marginatus
ticks in Central Slovakia (Brezina et al., 1969). After the first evidence
of this agent in vector ticks, several patients with clinical signs similar
to those associated with R. slovaca infection, confirmed in a French
patient in 2003, have been reported (Parola et al., 2009; Cascio et al.,
2013). Based on the most significant clinical symptoms in affected
patients, such as eschar and cervical lymphadenopathies, several names
have been proposed for diseases resulting from human infections, e.g.
tick-borne lymphadenopathy (TIBOLA), Dermacentor-borne necrosis-
erythrema-lymphadenopathy (DEBONEL) and/or scalp eschar and neck
lymphadenopathy (SENLAT) (Lakos, 1997, 1999; Oteo et al., 2003;
Angelakis et al., 2010). The peak incidence of human rickettsioses
usually occurs from March to May and during September and No-
vember, except the dry summer season, and this is clearly connected
with the seasonal activity of Dermacentor ticks (Estrada-Peña et al.,
2004; Parola et al., 2009).
In Slovakia, the Ixodes ricinus tick is considered the main vector and
natural reservoir of R. helvetica (Špitalská et al., 2008, 2014; Sekeyová
Rickettsia felis is primarily associated with an arthropod reservoir
and vector, the cat flea Ctenocephalides felis. It causes infection in hu-
mans, known as flea-borne spotted fever or cat-flea typhus (Abdad
et al., 2011). In Slovakia, Rickettsia sp. closely related to R. felis was
detected for the first time in a Ctenophthalmus solutus flea removed from
a striped field mouse (A. agrarius) (Špitalská et al., 2015).
In Slovakia, research on rickettsiae has a long tradition (Sekeyová
et al., 2013), but the role of rodents in their circulation has been much
less studied by molecular methods so far. Recently, only a few studies
referring to the presence of R. helvetica and R. monacensis in Apodemus
flavicollis and/or M. arvalis (Minichová et al., 2017), and Rickettsia spp.
in M. arvalis (Smetanová et al., 2006) have been published.
In the works of Jablonskaja (1978), R. slovaca was found in three
dominant rodent species, A. agrarius, A. flavicollis and M. arvalis, in
Eastern Slovakia; however, these results were only based on serological
analysis and cross-immunity studies, without further molecular evi-
dence. Řeháček et al. (1972), have also confirmed the presence of an-
tibodies against R. slovaca by serological analysis in small mammals
from Slovakia.
Until now, mostly experimental studies of rickettsial infection of A.
flavicollis, Clethrionomys glareolus, M. arvalis and Mus musculus, sus-
ceptibility and antibody formation were conducted in Slovakia
(Řehácek et al., 1976, 1992).
In order to update information on the occurrence and diversity of
rickettsiae, in the present study we focused on investigation of SFG
Rickettsia spp. in the wild small mammals from natural, suburban and
rural environments in eastern part of the country.
2. Material and methods

in Eastern Slovakia during the years 2014–2016. The first study site, a
Botanical garden with deciduous forest vegetation is located in the city

2.2. Rodents sampling
In total, 100 Swedish bridge metal traps filled with sunflower seeds
were set at each site, 5 m away from each other, for one night, and these
were checked next morning. Captured small mammals were transported
to the laboratory and euthanized in accordance with the licences of the
Ministry of Environment of the Slovak Republic No. 4874/2011–2.2
and 4559/2015–2.3. Subsequently, they were examined for the pre-
sence of ectoparasites, which were removed, collected and stored in
ethanol.
Each individual was identified into species, weighed with an accu-

condition of each animal was ascertained. Classification of mammals
into categories subadults (immature) and adults (mature) was used
according to Pelikán (1965) with respect to the sexual condition of
individuals. The removed ticks and other ectoparasites were de-
termined with the use of an identification key (Filippova, 1977), by
light microscopy. An ear biopsy was obtained from 245 animals and

2.4. Phylogenetic analysis
The obtained nucleotide sequences of Rickettsia spp. gltA gene
fragment were manually edited in MEGA 6 and compared with
GenBank entries by BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool)
(Tamura et al., 2013). Homologous sequences were aligned by the
ClustalW program.
The evolutionary history of the sequences was inferred by using the
Maximum Likelihood method based on the Tamura 3-parameter model
(Tamura, 1992). The best DNA substitution model was chosen by Model
Selection (ML) analysis. The tree with the highest log likelihood is
shown (Fig. 1).
2.5. Statistical analysis
The associations between the prevalences of rickettsiae in males and
females of the most abundant rodent species and the variation of sea-
sonal rickettsial occurrence in rodents were evaluated by the Fisher's
exact test using Past version 2.17b software (Hammer et al., 2001). A p
value
was considered to be statistically significant.

4. Discussion
Small mammals are associated with several pathogenic micro-
organisms and host a wide spectrum of ectoparasites. Some species of
rodents (e.g. A. flavicollis) in particular are more heavily infested with
Ixodes spp. ticks than others (Stanko and Miklisová, 2000). In general, a
different composition of rodent species was found in individual habi-
tats, suggesting that the character of the environment and the structure
of habitat considerably influence the composition of the hosts and their
ectoparasites. In total, 250 individuals of 11 species were captured,
with A. agrarius and A. flavicollis being the most prevalent species at all
three sampling sites during a three-year study.
Similarly, as it has been observed in the present study, the two
above-mentioned Apodemus species prevailed in the lowland habitats of
eastern Slovakia even in the past (Stanko and Miklisová, 2000). M.
glareolus was absent only in the urban environment, in the botanical
garden. The highest diversity of murid species as well as the highest
diversity of tick species feeding on rodents was observed in the natural
habitat, in the Slovak Karst National Park region. In addition, M. arvalis
occurred solely at this natural site, preferring pastures with shrubs.
In this study, the wild small mammals were screened for the pre-
sence of Rickettsia spp. in three different types of habitat in eastern
Slovakia. The highest prevalence of Rickettsia spp. was observed in ro-
dents captured in the suburban habitat. Rickettsial DNA was detected in
ear samples of small mammals belonging to six species, namely A.
agrarius, A. flavicollis, A. uralensis, M. glareolus, M. arvalis, and C. leu-
codon. Rickettsia sp. closely related to R. felis and two pathogenic spe-
cies, R. helvetica and R. slovaca, were identified in A. agrarius, A. flavi-
collis, M. glareolus and M. arvalis.
The highest prevalence of rickettsiae was recorded in M. glareolus
(13/58), followed by A. flavicollis (10/99). Only one rodent species,
specifically A. flavicollis captured in the suburban and rural areas,
carried DNA of different Rickettsia species (R. helvetica, R. slovaca, and
Rickettsia sp. closely related to R. felis), suggesting that some species of
rodents might play a more important role as hosts for different rick-
ettsiae. The data indicate that bank voles and yellow-necked mice are
probably more often infected with rickettsiae than other species of
rodents.
Rickettsiae are considered to be emerging or re-emerging patho-
gens, and there are limited data on their presence and prevalence in
many regions of Europe (Sprong et al., 2009). Up to now, several cases
of human rickettsioses have been recorded in Hungary (Lakos, 1997),
France (Raoult and Roux, 1997; Raoult et al., 2002), Sweden (Nilsson
et al., 1999, 2010), Switzerland (Baumann et al., 2003), Bulgaria
(Komitova et al., 2003), Portugal (de Sousa et al., 2006, 2008), Italy
(Selmi et al., 2008), Spain (Aguirrebengoa et al., 2008), Poland (Świtaj
et al., 2012) and Slovakia (Sekeyová et al., 2012).

Among the successfully genotyped samples, R. helvetica was the
most prevalent species recorded in small mammals at two sampling
sites, followed by Rickettsia sp. closely related to R. fellis. R. slovaca was
confirmed in one of successfully sequenced samples.
In study from Poland (Biernat et al., 2016) none of the examined A.
flavicollis and M. glareolus blood samples tested were positive for Rick-
ettsia spp., but rickettsial DNA was identified in rodent-attached I. ri-
cinus ticks. The authors suggested a very short-lasting rickettsiemia in
small mammals or the possibility of vertical transmission of infection.
The presence of R. slovaca was originally confirmed in vector ticks
D. marginatus and D. reticulatus (Brezina et al., 1969; Špitalská et al.,
2012; Minichová et al., 2017). As mentioned in the introduction, R.
slovaca was identified in ticks and small mammals by serological or
microscopic methods in the past, but our study represents the first
molecular evidence of R. slovaca in wild small mammals in Slovakia. In
our study, R. slovaca was detected in A. flavicollis captured in the Slovak
Karst region, where the sympatric occurrence of D. marginatus and D.
reticulatus ticks, the main vectors of R. slovaca, is quite common. A
previous examination of a smaller sample of D. reticulatus ticks from the
same area, Slovak Karst (Hrhov village) region, confirmed
prevalence of rickettsiae in adult ticks. Among other species of rick-
ettsiae, the presence of R. slovaca was recorded too (Radzijevskaja et al.,
2015). We assume a higher occurrence of R. slovaca in small mammals
(and other potential vertebrate hosts), especially in areas with the
presence of D. marginatus and D. reticulatus ticks. Species composition of
vectors and their hosts influence the occurrence and distribution of
pathogens in the studied area.
To analyze the tick species composition and the dominance of in-
dividual tick species on small mammals in detail was not the aim of this
study. However, the presence of several tick species, e.g. Ixodes spp.,
Dermacentor spp. and Haemaphysalis spp. on small mammals in the
Slovak Karst region, reflects the sympatric occurrence of distinct tick
species at the sampling site. This fact has already been published in the
past (e.g., Nosek, 1971, 1972; Hubálek, 1986, and others).
The investigation of small-mammal populations for the presence of
parasites and pathogens can help to improve knowledge about the oc-
currence, circulation and spreading of infectious agents in a specific
area. The data obtained in this study suggest that small mammals,
mainly some predominant species (e.g. Apodemus spp., Myodes spp.),
might play a more important role in the maintenance, circulation and
dissemination of rickettsiae within and outside the natural foci. The
prevalence of rickettsiae in small mammals depends on the type of
habitat, species composition and seasonal activity of vectors and

The herein presented results suggest a higher risk of infection with
zoonotic pathogens, R. helvetica and R. slovaca in natural and suburban
habitats of Eastern Slovakia, especially during the spring and autumn
season.
5. Conclusion
The presence of R. helvetica, R. slovaca and Rickettsia sp. closely
related to R. felis was confirmed in small mammals in Eastern Slovakia.
R. helvetica was found to be the predominantly occuring species in the
two investigated sites from several host species. R. slovaca was detected
in A. flavicollis captured in the Slovak Karst region, where the sympatric
occurrence of D. marginatus and D. reticulatus ticks is confirmed. We
assume the presence of R. slovaca especially in sites with the occurrence
of Dermacentor spp. In this study, Rickettsia sp. closely related to R. felis
was first time detected in A. flavicollis in suburban site of Slovakia.
Some rodent species that have a wider ecological valency may con-
tribute to the maintenance, circulation and dissemination of rickettsiae
within and out the natural foci more significantly than those species
that have narrower relation to the certain type of habitat.
The yellow-necked mouse (A. flavicollis) might be an important re-
servoir host of different Rickettsia spp., not only in Slovakia.
